claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved plastic strain relative to commercially used pure tungsten at high temperature.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten at high temperature.
Fine, ductile intergranular secondary phases form in equimolar WTaTiVZr.
The intergranular secondary phases facilitate grain-boundary sliding.
The intergranular secondary phases enhance dislocation mobility at high temperatures.
Ta, Ti, V, and Zr alloying produces the proposed precipitates or intergranular phases in WTaTiVZr.
Alloying in WTaTiVZr induces local compositional fluctuations.
Local compositional fluctuations stabilize ductile secondary phases along grain boundaries.
The secondary phases reduce brittle grain-boundary failure by facilitating grain-boundary sliding and alleviating stress concentrations.
Stress-concentration alleviation by the secondary phases enhances dislocation motion at high temperature.
Under matched high-temperature mechanical testing, WTaTiVZr will exhibit significantly greater plastic strain than pure tungsten.
Under matched high-temperature mechanical testing, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater fracture energy and delayed crack propagation relative to pure tungsten.
The proposed ductile intergranular phases will be observable after deformation in WTaTiVZr and absent in pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten has a more homogeneous and brittle grain-boundary structure that produces lower plastic strain and toughness.
The proposed mechanism applies at high, service-relevant temperatures and strain rates.
At lower temperatures or substantially different deformation conditions, mechanisms other than the proposed intergranular-phase mechanism may dominate.
